summary: Asks IANA to create a registry for fields in the IGMP message header and gives guidance for assigning values. It is a Best Current Practice. It was replaced by RFC 9778.

plainLanguage.summary: A club keeps a list so nobody picks the same number twice. This sets up that list for the multicast group-joining messages. It has been replaced by RFC 9778.

subtitle: Setting up a registry for IGMP message type codes

tldr.problem: The IGMP protocol has header fields (Type and Code) that need to be assigned by IANA, but there was no formal registry to manage these assignments and prevent duplicates.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3228 asks IANA to create a registry for IGMP Type and Code values, with clear rules: Type values use IESG Approval or Standards Action, and Code values follow policies set in the RFC defining the new Type.
tldr.outcome: A structured registry prevents conflicting assignments and makes the protocol extensible. RFC 3228 was later replaced by RFC 9778.

today: RFC 3228 is Historic. It was superseded by RFC 9778, which provides updated IANA considerations for IGMP.

sections.title: What the RFC Does
sections.content:
RFC 3228 is a Best Current Practice that asks IANA to create and manage a registry for fields in the IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) header. IGMP lets programs tell a network they want to receive multicast messages sent to a group.

The IGMP header contains two kinds of values that IANA must manage: Type (which kind of IGMP message) and Code (which subtype or behavior for that Type). Without a clear registry, two different RFCs might assign the same value to different uses, breaking the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: IGMP messages have labels and codes. This RFC says someone official should keep a list of what each label and code means, so two people don't both pick the number 5 for their own idea.

sections.title: How IANA Assigns Type and Code Values
sections.content:
New Type values are assigned only through IESG Approval (Internet Engineering Steering Group approves) or Standards Action (the value is defined in a Standards Track RFC). Code values for existing Types follow the same rule unless the RFC defining that Type says otherwise.

The key insight is that different Types can have different Code policies. When an RFC introduces a new Type, it can specify in that same RFC how Code values for that Type will be allocated.
sections.plainLanguage: New labels need official approval from important people. Each label can have its own rules for its codes, written in the RFC that first uses that label.

sections.title: Codes Reserved for Testing
sections.content:
IGMP Code values 240 to 255 (in hexadecimal: 0xf0 to 0xff) are reserved for protocol testing and experimentation. Systems that receive IGMP messages with unknown Code values must silently ignore them, rather than treating them as errors.

This reserve encourages engineers to experiment safely without corrupting the production protocol, and the silent-ignore rule prevents cascading failures when an experimental code reaches a system that has not been updated to recognize it.
sections.plainLanguage: There are special test numbers (240-255) that engineers can use to try new ideas. If a program gets a message with a number it doesn't recognize, it just ignores it quietly rather than crashing.

sections.title: Why This Matters for Security
sections.content:
Network firewalls and intrusion detection systems monitor IGMP traffic to spot attacks. If a new Type or Code value is assigned but the security tool doesn't yet understand it, the tool might either block the traffic (breaking service) or pass it through without checking (opening a security hole).

This is why RFC 3228 says new Type values should go through Standards Action or IESG Approval: the visibility ensures security tools have time to understand the change before the new value is widely used.
sections.plainLanguage: When something new gets a number, people protecting the network need to know about it soon, or their guards might accidentally block it or let bad things through.
